newsitem.title: USA: U.S. MUNICIPAL FOCUS -- pedaling up from lows.
newsitem.headline: U.S. MUNICIPAL FOCUS -- pedaling up from lows.

text.p: U.S. municipal bonds pedaled up from lows as shortcovering late Monday helped Treasury bonds trim nearly a full point loss, hit after the latest data surprised the market by depicting a more vigorous economy.
Municipal bonds were pegged at down 1/4 to 3/8 of a point, up slightly from the 3/8 level seen earlier.

The latest premium paid for buying security against inflation was 188 points over the six-month change in the Consumer Price Index, as seen in an offering by the Delaware Finance Authority, which sold about $70 million of debt that matures in 2027 at that price.
"Basically, we had been working in the 185 area," said Paul Kuhns, manager, municipal syndicate desk, Merrill Lynch. The firm underwrote the offering.

Institutional investors, the main buyers of the new debt, got a few basis points more in yield than some of the first offerings linked to the CPI. But buyers who were willing to go further out the yield curve naturally snared the biggest premium, with the spread over the CPI change seen at roughly 210 points for some hospital paper, he added.
The Authority sold a total of $140 million of debt, and the offering was repriced to yield 5.75 percent in 2027.

Traders said that fundamentals in the municipal market looked weaker, noting the 30-day supply calender as well as the Standard and Poor's Corp Blue List, a gauge of the secondary market, were starting to look heavy.
The Blue List stands at $1.6 billion, a level higher than in recent months.

In the secondary market, Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority Massachusetts General Transportation of 2023, which pay a five percent coupon, were bid at 5.63 percent, NET, up three basis points.
And Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, Sanitary Authority Sewer Revenues of 2024, which pay a 5-3/8 percent coupon, were bid at 5.66 percent, NET, also up three basis points.

The latest economic data reawakened jitters that either the Federal Reserve, whose policy making arm begins a two-day meeting on Tuesday, or the June payrolls data, which can sharply affect prices, would not fulfill expectations.
Economists have predicted the central bank would leave rates unchanged, and they look for companies to have added 222,000 jobs.

Among the data depressing prices was the Chicago Purchasers Index, which jumped to 61.5 in June, sharply higher than forecasts for a slight drop from May's 56.8 level to 56.4. An index below 50 signals a slowing manufacturing economy, while a reading above 50 points to an expansion.

And a big uptick in May home sales also hurt, as they rose 7.1 percent to an annual rate of 825,000. Only a rate of 786,000 units had been expected. And May's 4.1 months' supply of homes for sales was the lowest amount since March 1971.

The September municipal bond futures closed down 10 ticks at 116-16/32, while the September Treasury bond futures shed 18 ticks to 111-2/32. This left the MOB spread at plus 174 ticks, firmer by eight ticks than levels seen late Friday.
